title: A Great Many Socks

pages.text:
*From the Dropout Club Handbook, Rule 4: Socks are not a spell. Socks are a lifestyle.*

Marnie and Toby scrambled up through a drift of wool that felt suspiciously like a snowdrift, except it smelled of laundry soap and regret. There were stripy socks, polka-dot socks, and one grey sock with a hole shaped exactly like the country of France.

Marnie pulled a striped sock off her head. She was now looking at a girl who was slowly climbing down from a rafter.

The girl had a black braid that reached her knees, tied with a pink ribbon. She wore an orange hoodie and mismatched socks, one striped and one dotted, which was odd given the situation.

"I'm so, so sorry," the girl said, her voice trembling. "I'm so, so, so sorry. I was trying to make a candle. It was a candle yesterday too. And the day before. It's always a candle I mean to make."

Marnie looked at the pile of socks. She looked at the girl. She looked at the one sock with the French hole.

"A candle," Marnie repeated. Her voice climbed to a pitch she did not recognize as her own.

"Yes," said the girl, hanging upside down from the rafter. Her hair defied gravity with a dignity that seemed personally offensive to Marnie. "A very nice, bright, useful candle."
pages.image: Inside a dim wooden shed, a girl with a long black braid and orange hoodie hangs upside down from a rafter, looking apologetic, while below her a girl with copper-red hair buns and a boy with glasses stand buried up to their chins in a massive heap of colorful mismatched socks.

pages.text:
Her name was Lulu Vasquez. She was ten years old, which made her the youngest student Humbleton Academy had ever admitted, a fact that usually came with a plaque in the lobby. Instead, it had come with a hammock and a steady diet of cheese sandwiches.

"Rain spell?" Marnie asked, holding up a wet, lavender-scented sock.

"Socks," Lulu said. "Flying spell? Socks. I cast 'Ignis' once, just to be polite, and I got a heap of lavender socks that smelled like my aunt’s garden."

Toby adjusted his glasses, looking at the socks with the critical eye of an auditor reviewing a bad invoice. "Your teacher," he said, "did not find this polite."

Lulu winced. "She said, 'Miss Vasquez, this academy is not a laundry.'" She shrank into her hoodie. "I was too embarrassed to go home. So I’ve been sleeping in the hammock for nine days. Toby brings me sandwiches. He’s very good at that. He doesn’t even complain about the socks."

Toby picked up a polka-dot sock, sniffed it, and dropped it. "It is very consistent," he said softly. "That is rare."

Marnie looked at her own hands. They were still sticky from the cheese. She felt a strange, warm feeling in her chest, like a cat sleeping in a sunbeam.
pages.image: In a cozy corner of the shed, a boy in a navy vest and bow tie holds a cheese sandwich, while a girl in an orange hoodie looks shy and embarrassed, surrounded by a neat stack of lavender-smelling socks on a wooden table.

pages.text:
The socks were never pairs, a fact for which Lulu apologized with the same regularity she produced them, as if she were personally responsible for the invention of mismatching. Toby, however, pointed out with quiet precision that consistency was a form of magic. If your spells always produced socks, then you were a sock wizard. It was a niche, certainly, but it was yours.

Above them, the rafters were carved with names. Marnie reached up and traced the deep scratches in the wood, her finger following the grooves where other students had marked their time in the shed.

"Ermintrude, 1743: turned my own nose into a turnip," she read aloud.

"Barnaby: my wand exploded (twice)," Toby added, reading the next one.

There were hundreds of them. Three hundred years of students who had been told their magic was wrong, and who had come here, to this shed, to sit in the dark and be wrong together. The shed had always been the place for the failures, yet the air inside felt less like a punishment and more like a refuge.

Marnie looked at the carvings, then at Lulu, then at Toby. The feeling in her chest shifted, settling into something solid and warm, like a stone that had finally found its spot in a wall. She was not a mistake. She was simply different.
pages.image: Close up on a wooden rafter with deep, old carved names and dates, illuminated by a warm lantern light, while a girl with freckles and a boy with glasses look up at the carvings with wide, amazed eyes.

pages.text:
Marnie laughed. It was a real laugh, the kind that starts in your belly and ends with a wet snort. She laughed until her eyes stung and her ribs ached from the sheer effort of it.

Lulu watched her, her long black braid swinging gently against her orange hoodie. Then, with great solemnity, she reached into the lavender-scented heap and pulled out a single sock. It was a soft, mossy green, with a hole right in the toe.

"For you," Lulu said. "A welcome gift. It’s all I can do."

Marnie took the sock. It was soft and warm. She looked at the hole, then at Lulu, and then she said, "It’s the nicest present I’ve ever had."

And she meant it. It tingled in her teeth and her fingertips. She tucked the sock into her cardigan pocket, right next to her pencil.

Toby nodded, pushing up his glasses with approval. "Acceptable," he said.

Marnie smiled. For the first time in two years, her magic didn’t feel like a curse. It felt like a tool. A strange, socks-and-geese kind of tool, but a tool all the same.
pages.image: A close-up of a girl's freckled hand holding a soft green sock with a hole in the toe, while another girl with a long braid smiles warmly, and a boy with gold glasses looks on with a gentle, approving expression.

pages.text:
The silence in the shed was thick and comfortable, broken only by the soft tick of the clock and the occasional squawk of the goose. Marnie was just about to suggest a rule about who got the last biscuit when the door creaked.

It wasn’t a normal creak, though. It was a groan, a deep, wooden protest that shook the dust from the rafters. The entire shed tilted to the left, just slightly, as if someone enormous had leaned against it.

Lulu went pale. "Oh," she whispered. "That’ll be Bunt."

A hand pushed through the door. It was the size of a coal shovel, grey-green, and holding a silver tray. On the tray sat a tower of biscuits, stacked so high they defied gravity. The hand wiggled, and the biscuits clattered pleasantly.

Marnie looked at Toby. Toby looked at Lulu.

"We’re not alone," Marnie said, her voice small.

No. They were definitely not alone. And the door was opening wider.
pages.image: A massive, grey-green hand the size of a shovel pushes through a small wooden door, holding a silver tray stacked high with round biscuits, while three small children inside the shed look up in awe and surprise, with Gerald nearby.
